title: Where exactly do you put the probe in a chicken?
desc: The USDA names three places to check a whole bird and one thing to avoid. Here is the placement map, and what it means for the two thermometers in this shop.
image_caption: Editorial illustration. Not a product photograph.
body:
A thermometer can be accurate and still mislead you: the USDA's food thermometer factsheet states that the reading is only correct if the probe sits in the right part of the food. For a whole bird it names the places — and the one thing to stay away from — in plain words. This page turns that guidance into a placement map you can use at the oven door, then connects it to the two thermometers in this shop.

The USDA placement map for whole poultry

Verbatim from the factsheet: “When cooking whole poultry, check the internal temperature in three places: the innermost part of the thigh, the innermost part of the wing and the thickest part of the breast. Avoid the bone.”

WhereWhat the USDA saysSource
Innermost part of the thighOne of the three places to check a whole bird.USDA FSIS, Food Thermometers
Innermost part of the wingOne of the three places to check a whole bird.USDA FSIS, Food Thermometers
Thickest part of the breastOne of the three places to check a whole bird.USDA FSIS, Food Thermometers
What to avoidAvoid the bone — bone conducts heat and reads hotter than the meat around it.USDA FSIS, Food Thermometers
Poultry parts (breasts, thighs, wings)Insert into the thickest area, avoiding the bone; for thin pieces, go in through the side so the sensing area reaches the centre.USDA FSIS, Food Thermometers
Stuffing“For optimum safety, do not stuff whole poultry.” If you do, the centre of the stuffing must reach 165 °F.USDA FSIS, Food Thermometers
Target temperatureAll poultry — whole bird, breasts, thighs, wings, ground poultry, giblets, stuffing — has a safe minimum internal temperature of 165 °F (73.9 °C).USDA FSIS safe-temperature chart

Placement and stuffing wording quoted from the USDA FSIS “Food Thermometers” factsheet; the 165 °F minimum from the FSIS safe-temperature chart. Both fetched and read on 2026-11-20.

What this means for the two thermometers in this shop

SituationWhat the listing saysSource
Checking the three places quicklyAn instant-read suits the three-point check: the ThermoMaven listing states a 1-second read and a fold-out probe, so you can move between thigh, wing and breast without holding the oven door open.B0DHZTCNR5
One probe left in while it cooksThe CHEF iQ Sense listing states three ultra-thin probes and a wireless hub, so separate probes can sit in breast and thigh at the same time. Its stated 1000 °F heat-safe figure is the seller's own claim — read it on the listing.B0DZFD6R9Z
Reading the probe depthThe USDA says to follow the manufacturer's instructions for how deep the probe must sit; the wireless category in the USDA's own table is “designed to remain in the food while it is cooking” at least 1 inch deep in the thickest part.USDA FSIS, Food Thermometers
Cleaning up after the birdThe USDA's care guidance: wash with hot, soapy water, and most thermometers should not be immersed in water.USDA FSIS, Food Thermometers

Product behaviour is described only by what each listing states (B0DHZTCNR5, B0DZFD6R9Z, read 2026-11-20); placement and care guidance is the USDA's. Accuracy figures, heat limits and probe counts are seller claims, not measurements taken here.

The decision shortcut. If you check a bird once or twice a season, the three-point check with an instant-read is the USDA's own method and needs no app. If you monitor long cooks without opening the door, that is the case the wireless unit was designed for — and the placement rules do not change.

faq: Where do you put a meat thermometer in a whole chicken?

The USDA says to check a whole bird in three places: the innermost part of the thigh, the innermost part of the wing, and the thickest part of the breast — avoiding the bone. Each row on this page quotes the source.
What temperature does chicken need to reach?
All poultry has a safe minimum internal temperature of 165 degrees F (73.9 degrees C) on the USDA FSIS safe-temperature chart, including whole bird, parts, ground poultry and stuffing.
Can I leave the probe in the chicken while it cooks?

Only with a thermometer designed for it. The USDA's own table says wireless/smart thermometers are designed to remain in the food while cooking; its care section warns not to leave a thermometer in food unless the manufacturer says it can withstand heat. The wireless listing in this shop claims a 1000 degrees F heat-safe probe - a seller claim, linked above.
Does the probe touch the bone change the reading?
Yes - that is exactly what the USDA's 'avoid the bone' instruction is about. Bone conducts heat, so a probe resting against it can read hotter than the meat around it and stop you early.
